passages.happening:
“At this my heart also pounds and leaps from its place. Listen closely to the thunder of His voice and the rumbling that comes from His mouth” (verses 1-2). God lets loose his lightning under the whole sky. ‘God thunders wondrously with His voice; He does great things we cannot comprehend’ (verse 5).

He tells the snow to fall and the rain to pour. He seals up every person's hand from work, ‘so that all men may know His work’ (verse 7). The animals go to their dens. The storm comes from its chamber and the cold from the north. ‘By the breath of God the ice is formed and the watery expanses are frozen’ (verse 10). The clouds whirl at his direction. ‘Whether for punishment or for His land, He accomplishes this in His loving devotion’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Elihu describes a storm as if it were breaking while he speaks, his own heart pounding. The word voice comes again and again: God's thunder is God speaking.

In the lands around Israel, the storm was the clearest display of divine power, and storm gods held a leading place. In the Canaanite texts from Ugarit, written before 1200 BC, Baal is the storm god who thunders with his voice and gives the rain. Elihu gives all of it to the one God. For an ancient reader that stripped the storm of any rival god. The thunder is simply the voice of the Creator.

For people who worked the land, weather was life and death. Snow and heavy rain stopped work in the fields and drove animals into their dens. Verse 13 uses chesed, God's covenant love. In a world that often read storms and floods as signs of anger, Elihu says the same weather can serve discipline, the good of the land, or God's steadfast love.
passages.later: A psalm hears the same voice in the storm: “The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders; the LORD is heard over many waters” (Psalm 29:3).
passages.hard:
Does God cause every storm and natural disaster?

Elihu speaks as though God directly commands every snowfall and lightning strike, and much of the Old Testament speaks the same way. Readers have understood this differently. Many Christians, in the Reformed tradition especially, hold that God's providence governs all events, natural ones included, though through ordinary causes and for purposes people often cannot see. Others stress that creation has a real freedom and regularity of its own, and that the Bible's language of God sending rain and snow affirms his final rule without making him the immediate cause of each event in a mechanical way.

What Elihu adds is purpose: a storm may come for discipline, for the good of the land, or from God's steadfast love. He does not claim that anyone can tell which is which in a given case. The book of Job as a whole warns against reading any particular disaster as a verdict on the people it strikes. Job's own children died in a storm (1:19), and the reader knows it was not their punishment.
passages.asks: Elihu heard God's voice in the thunder. Ask what in creation makes you aware of God. And ask how you would talk with a neighbor whose home a storm has destroyed, without claiming to know why it came.

passages.happening:
“Listen to this, O Job; stand still and consider the wonders of God” (verse 14). Does Job know how God sends the clouds or makes the lightning flash, or how the clouds float? Job, whose clothes are hot when the south wind hushes the land, can he spread out the sky like a mirror of bronze?

“Teach us what we should say to Him; we cannot draw up our case when our faces are in darkness” (verse 19).

No one can look at the sun when the wind has swept the sky clean. ‘Out of the north He comes in golden splendor; awesome majesty surrounds Him’ (verse 22). “The Almighty is beyond our reach; He is exalted in power! In His justice and great righteousness He does not oppress. Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart” (verses 23-24).
passages.hearers:
The south wind was the hot, dry wind from the desert, known for its stifling heat. Mirrors were made of polished metal, not glass, and a sky like a mirror of bronze is the hard, shining dome of a cloudless summer sky.

Elihu's questions to Job, do you know, do you understand, can you, look ahead to the form of God's own speech, which is almost all questions.

North in verse 22 is tsaphon, the word that was also the name of the mountain of Baal in the Canaanite texts. Elihu says it is God who comes from there in golden splendor.

This chapter closes the whole human side of the debate. Job, the three friends and Elihu have all spoken, and each has tried to account for God. Elihu's last words point beyond himself, to a God beyond reach. The very next verse in the book says that the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind.
passages.asks: Elihu told Job to stand still and consider. Ask when you last did that, with no argument to win. And ask what it would mean for you to wait for God to speak, rather than speaking for him.
